paper.title: Known Unknowns: Out-of-Distribution Property Prediction in Materials and Molecules
paper.research_summary: Our objective is to train predictor models that extrapolate zero-shot to higher ranges than in the training data, given the chemical compositions of solids or molecular graphs and their property values. We propose using a transductive approach to OOD property prediction, achieving improvements in prediction accuracy. In particular, our method improves extrapolative precision by 1.8× for materials and 1.5× for molecules, and boosts recall of high-performing candidates by up to 3×. Our method leverages analogical input-target relations in the training and test sets, enabling generalization beyond the training target support, and can be applied to any other material and molecular tasks.

output_goal: predicted property values for OOD candidates

stages.stage_name_raw: Curating benchmark datasets for solid materials and molecules
stages.stage_goal: Acquire diverse, high-throughput computational and experimental datasets covering multiple material properties for evaluation.

evidence.text: We evaluate the extrapolation capability of Bilinear Transduction on three widely used benchmarks for solid materials property prediction, AFLOW, Matbench, and the Materials Project (MP), covering 12 distinct prediction tasks of various classes of materials properties: electronic, mechanical, thermal, etc.

For molecular systems, we used datasets from MoleculeNet, covering four graph-to-property prediction tasks with dataset sizes ranging from 600 to 4200 samples, and benchmarked our approach against three baseline methods.

stages.stage_name_raw: Preprocessing datasets to define ID and OOD splits
stages.stage_goal: Split data into training, validation, and test sets such that OOD test samples are the top 5% of property values, ID validation set is a random 5% of remaining data, and training set is the rest.

evidence.text: We split the data into training, validation and test sets such that OOD test samples Dte Y  Y are 5% of the data with the highest property values, an ID validation set is a random sample of 5% of the remaining data, and the training set Dtr ¼ fðx; yÞgn  X × Y is the rest.

stages.stage_name_raw: Training Bilinear Transduction model on composition/graph representations
stages.stage_goal: Train a bilinear transductive predictor hθ(Δx, x) = fθ(Δx)gθ(x) to learn how property values change as a function of material/molecular differences rather than predicting values directly.
stage_input: training set with stoichiometry-based representations for solids and RDKit descriptors for molecules

evidence.text: During training, rather than predicting hθ : X ! Y, predictor hθ : ΔX × X ! Y predicts value y2 2 Dtr Y for data point x2 2 Dtr X given anchor point x1 2 Dtr X and the difference between them Δx21 ¼ x2  x1 2 Dtr ΔX.
The predictor hθ(Δx, x) = fθ(Δx)gθ(x) is implemented as a bilinear function in non-linear embeddings of Δx and x.

stages.stage_name_raw: Screening large candidate databases for high-performing OOD candidates
stages.stage_goal: Identify high-performing OOD candidates from a set of known compositions/molecular graphs with unknown properties using predicted property values and thresholding.
stage_output: top OOD candidates (e.g., top 30% of test samples with highest property values)

evidence.text: In this case, the objective is to identify high-performing OOD candidates from a set of known compositions with unknown properties. Screening often involves applying a threshold, either an absolute value or a percentile cutoff, and selecting candidates whose predicted properties exceed it.

In addition, we report model performance on a purely extrapolative task of discovering high-performance extremes: identifying the 30% of test samples with the highest property values, which we refer to as the top OOD candidates.

stages.stage_name_raw: Evaluating OOD prediction accuracy and extrapolative precision/recall
stages.stage_goal: Quantitatively assess model performance on OOD test sets using metrics including mean absolute error (MAE), extrapolative precision, and recall of high-performing candidates.

evidence.text: Table 1 presents the mean absolute error (MAE) for OOD predictions on solids, showing that Bilinear Transduction consistently outperforms or performs comparably to the baseline methods across tasks.
Table 2 presents the fraction of true top OOD candidates correctly identified among the top predicted candidates, reflecting improved precision in retrieving extreme-value molecules.
Bilinear Transduction boosts recall of OOD materials by 3 ×, compared with the best average recall score among the models presented in Table S2.

We evaluate the extrapolation capability of Bilinear Transduction on three widely used benchmarks for solid materials property prediction, AFLOW, Matbench, and the Materials Project (MP), covering 12 distinct prediction tasks of various classes of materials properties: electronic, mechanical, thermal, etc.
AFLOW contains material property values obtained from high-throughput calculations30.

Following Kauwe et al.20, who evaluated classical ML algorithms on AFLOW, we curate a subset of six properties: band gap, bulk modulus, Debye temperature, shear modulus, thermal conductivity, and thermal expansion, out of which the last four are scaled by applying a base 10 logarithm.

We evaluate the extrapolation capability of Bilinear Transduction on three widely used benchmarks for solid materials property prediction, AFLOW, Matbench, and the Materials Project (MP), covering 12 distinct prediction tasks of various classes of materials properties: electronic, mechanical, thermal, etc.

Matbench is an automated leaderboard for benchmarking ML algorithms predicting solid material properties12. Matbench contains three composition-based regression tasks: experimentally measured band gap14, experimentally measured yield strength of steels31, calculated formation energy32, and calculated refractive index33.

We evaluate the extrapolation capability of Bilinear Transduction on three widely used benchmarks for solid materials property prediction, AFLOW, Matbench, and the Materials Project (MP), covering 12 distinct prediction tasks of various classes of materials properties: electronic, mechanical, thermal, etc.
MP provides materials and their property values derived from high-throughput calculations32.
Following Wang et al.13, we focus on bulk modulus, shear modulus, and the ratio of elastic anisotropy.

For molecular systems, we used datasets from MoleculeNet, covering four graph-to-property prediction tasks with dataset sizes ranging from 600 to 4200 samples, and benchmarked our approach against three baseline methods.
MoleculeNet includes molecular graphs encoded as SMILES representations35 and their property values derived from high-throughput calculations and experimental trials36.

We focus on physical chemistry and biophysics properties suitable for regression tasks, using four benchmark datasets from MoleculeNet. The ESOL dataset provides measurements of aqueous solubility for small molecules, FreeSolv contains experimental and calculated hydration free energies for small neutral molecules in water, Lipophilicity reports octanol/water distribution coefﬁcients, and BACE includes binding afﬁnities of small molecules to human β-secretase 1 (BACE-1).
